aphids.description: Small soft-bodied insects that cluster on young shoots and the underside of leaves, sucking sap and spreading plant viruses.
identification: Pear-shaped insects 1-3 mm long, green, black or grey
Two small tube-like 'cornicles' at the rear
Dense colonies, often tended by ants
symptoms: Black sooty mould growing on honeydew
aphids.lifecycle: Females give birth to live young without mating; a new generation every 7-10 days in warm weather. Winged forms appear when colonies get crowded.

cultural: Remove heavily infested shoots
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertiliser
Control weeds that host aphids
Wash colonies off with a strong water spray
biological: Conserve ladybird beetles, lacewings and hoverflies
Neem oil or mild soap solution sprays
Yellow sticky traps to monitor winged aphids
chemical: Treat only when colonies are spreading and natural enemies are few
Use registered products and target the underside of leaves
Avoid broad-spectrum sprays that kill beneficial insects

edibility.reason: Aphids and their sticky honeydew sit on the surface; they are not poisonous.
advice: Wash leaves and pods well in clean water
Discard badly curled or mouldy parts

aspergillus_mould.description: A mould that grows on maize and groundnuts in the field and in storage and produces aflatoxin, a poison that causes liver damage and cancer. Aflatoxin is not destroyed by cooking.
identification: Olive-green to yellow-green powdery mould on kernels or nuts
Often on insect-damaged or cracked grain
Musty smell
symptoms: Green-yellow mould on cobs, kernels or nuts
aspergillus_mould.lifecycle: Lives in soil and crop residue; infects through insect damage and drought stress; grows fast in grain stored damp (above about 13% moisture).

cultural: Harvest on time and dry grain quickly to below 13% moisture
Sort out mouldy, damaged and discoloured kernels or nuts
Store in clean, dry, hermetic bags off the floor
Control field insects that damage cobs
biological: Aflasafe biocontrol product applied in the field where available
chemical: No spray makes contaminated grain safe

edibility.reason: This mould can produce aflatoxin, a poison that damages the liver and causes cancer. Cooking does not destroy it.
advice: Do NOT eat mouldy kernels or nuts, and do not feed them to animals
Do not wash or sort mouldy grain to sell or eat; destroy it
Test stored grain if mould is found in a batch

cassava_bacterial_blight.description: A bacterial disease spread by infected cuttings, rain splash and tools. Most severe in the rainy season.
identification: Angular, water-soaked leaf spots
Wilting of leaves and shoot tips
Sticky gum oozing from stems
symptoms: Angular leaf spots that turn brown
cassava_bacterial_blight.lifecycle: Survives in infected stems and debris; spreads by rain splash, insects, contaminated tools and cuttings.

cultural: Use clean cuttings from healthy plants
Rotate crops and destroy infected debris
Disinfect cutting tools between plants
biological: Plant tolerant varieties
chemical: No effective field chemical control

edibility.reason: The bacterium attacks leaves and stems; roots are usually fine but can rot on badly affected plants.
advice: Use firm, white roots only; discard rotten or discoloured roots
Process cassava as usual

cassava_green_mite.description: A tiny green mite that feeds on young cassava leaves, especially in the dry season, and can reduce root yield considerably.
identification: Very small green mites (under 1 mm), best seen with a hand lens
Found on the underside of young leaves near the shoot tip
symptoms: Yellow chlorotic spots giving a mottled look
'Candlestick' appearance when top leaves drop off
cassava_green_mite.lifecycle: Egg → larva → two nymph stages → adult in about 1-2 weeks. Numbers rise rapidly in hot dry weather.

cultural: Use tolerant varieties with hairy leaves
Plant early in the rainy season
Avoid moving infested planting material
biological: Conserve the predatory mite Typhlodromalus aripo, which lives in the shoot tip
chemical: Acaricides are rarely recommended for cassava; biological control is preferred

cassava_green_mite.taxonomy: Animalia › Arthropoda › Arachnida › Acari › Trombidiformes › Tetranychidae

edibility.reason: Mites feed on leaves only; roots are not affected in quality.
advice: Peel and process cassava as usual
Wash cassava leaves well if eating them

cassava_mealybug.description: A pink, waxy mealybug that attacks cassava shoot tips during the dry season. It was brought under control in Africa by the parasitic wasp Anagyrus lopezi, one of the most successful biological control programmes ever.
identification: Pinkish oval insects covered in white powdery wax
Clusters at shoot tips and under leaves
White cottony egg sacs
symptoms: 'Bunchy top': shortened internodes and crowded leaves at the tip
cassava_mealybug.lifecycle: Reproduces without males; each female lays several hundred eggs. Populations explode in the dry season and crash with heavy rains.

cultural: Plant clean, mealybug-free stem cuttings
Plant early in the rainy season so plants are strong by the dry season
Remove and burn heavily infested tips
biological: Conserve the parasitoid Anagyrus lopezi and ladybird predators
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill these natural enemies
chemical: Dip cuttings in a registered treatment before planting if infestation is known
Field spraying is rarely economic; rely on biological control

edibility.reason: Mealybugs damage shoots and reduce yield; the roots stay safe to eat.
advice: Peel and process cassava as usual (soaking, fermenting or cooking) as with any cassava

cassava_mosaic_disease.description: The most damaging cassava disease in Africa. It spreads through infected stem cuttings and by whiteflies, and can cut root yield by more than half.
identification: Yellow and green mosaic pattern on leaves
Leaves twisted, puckered or reduced in size
Symptoms on all leaves of plants grown from infected cuttings
symptoms: Stunted plants and fewer, smaller roots
cassava_mosaic_disease.lifecycle: Carried in stem cuttings from infected plants and by Bemisia tabaci whiteflies feeding on healthy plants.

cultural: Plant resistant varieties and clean cuttings from healthy plants
Remove and destroy infected plants early (roguing)
Do not take cuttings from diseased fields
biological: Manage whitefly populations; conserve their natural enemies
chemical: No chemical cure for the virus

edibility.reason: Plant viruses do not infect people. Roots may be fewer and smaller but are safe.
advice: Peel and process cassava as usual (soaking, fermenting or cooking)

cocoa_black_pod.description: The most serious cocoa disease in Ghana, especially in wet months. Pods turn brown-black and the beans inside rot.
identification: Small brown spot on the pod that spreads quickly
Whole pod turns chocolate-brown to black
White fungal-like growth on the pod surface
symptoms: Pods may mummify on the tree
cocoa_black_pod.lifecycle: Survives in soil and on infected pods; spread by rain splash, ants and contaminated tools during the rainy season.

cultural: Remove and bury infected pods weekly
Harvest ripe pods frequently
Prune for air flow and reduce shade
Improve drainage
biological: Keep the farm clean of infected husks
chemical: Follow the COCOBOD / CRIG spraying calendar with approved fungicides

edibility.reason: Beans inside black pods rot and must not be used for food.
advice: Do not use beans from black or rotting pods
Beans from healthy pods are fine

cocoa_mirid.description: The most important insect pest of cocoa in Ghana. Mirids pierce pods and young shoots, and the wounds are then invaded by fungi.
identification: Reddish-brown to dark bugs about 10 mm long with long antennae
Nymphs are smaller and wingless
Mostly active at night and hide during the day
symptoms: Dark, oval, sunken lesions on pods
Blackened lesions on shoots that lead to dieback ('mirid blast')
cocoa_mirid.lifecycle: Eggs inserted into pod husks or stems → five nymph stages → adult; about 4-6 weeks. Populations peak from August to December.

cultural: Keep a uniform canopy and fill gaps; mirids favour sunny pockets
Prune and remove mistletoe and chupons
Regular inspection of pods and young shoots
biological: Conserve ants such as Oecophylla (weaver ants) which prey on mirids
chemical: Follow the COCOBOD / CRIG recommended spraying calendar and approved insecticides
Spray mainly August to December when populations peak

edibility.reason: Lesions on pods can let in fungi that rot the beans.
advice: Use beans only from sound pods
Discard pods with black, rotten or mouldy beans

diamondback_moth.description: The most destructive pest of cabbage worldwide, including in Ghana's vegetable-growing areas. It is notorious for insecticide resistance.
identification: Small green larvae up to 12 mm that wriggle backwards when touched
Larvae hang from a silk thread when disturbed
Adult moth has a row of diamond shapes along its back
symptoms: Small 'windowpane' holes where larvae eat one leaf surface
Damage to the growing point and heads
diamondback_moth.lifecycle: Egg → four larval instars (about 10-14 days) → pupa in a loose silk cocoon on the leaf → adult. Around 3 weeks per generation.

cultural: Crop rotation and removal of brassica residues
Overhead irrigation disrupts egg laying
Use healthy transplants from netted nurseries
biological: Bt biopesticides are very effective
Neem sprays
Conserve parasitoid wasps (Cotesia, Diadegma)
chemical: Resistance is widespread; rotate modes of action strictly and use only registered products

edibility.reason: Larvae and droppings get between cabbage leaves.
advice: Remove outer leaves, larvae and droppings
Wash thoroughly; discard heavily eaten or rotting heads

fall_armyworm.description: An invasive caterpillar that arrived in West Africa in 2016 and is now one of the most damaging pests of maize in Ghana. Larvae feed inside the whorl and can destroy young plants.
identification: Inverted pale 'Y' mark on the head of the larva
Four dark spots forming a square on the second-to-last body segment
Moist sawdust-like frass (droppings) in the whorl
symptoms: Ragged holes and torn leaves in the whorl
Frass in the funnel of the plant
Damaged tassels and cobs in heavy attacks
fall_armyworm.lifecycle: Egg (2-3 days) → Larva, 6 instars (14-22 days) → Pupa in soil (8-9 days) → Adult moth. Several generations per season; moths fly long distances.

cultural: Scout fields twice a week from emergence, checking 20 plants in a W pattern
Plant early and at the same time as neighbours
Hand-pick egg masses and young larvae
Intercrop maize with legumes; push-pull with Desmodium and Brachiaria
biological: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) and Spodoptera NPV biopesticides on young larvae
Neem-based sprays into the whorl
Conserve natural enemies such as earwigs, ants and parasitic wasps
chemical: Only when scouting shows more than about 20% of young plants damaged
Use products registered by Ghana EPA for fall armyworm and follow the label
Spray into the whorl early morning or late evening when larvae are active
Rotate modes of action to delay resistance

edibility.reason: Larvae chew leaves and cobs; damaged cobs can then grow harmful moulds.
advice: Remove larvae, frass and damaged kernels before eating
Throw away cobs that show any green or pink mould

grasshopper.description: A brightly coloured grasshopper that feeds on many crops and can strip cassava plants of leaves in the dry season.
identification: Black, yellow, orange and green markings
Nymphs cluster in groups on vegetation
Slow-moving; gives off an unpleasant smell when handled
symptoms: Leaves eaten from the edges inward
grasshopper.lifecycle: Eggs laid in soil pods (egg-laying sites are reused yearly) → nymphs hatch at the start of the dry season → adults after several moults. One generation per year.

cultural: Locate and dig up egg-laying sites in the rainy season
Destroy nymph clusters early in the morning
Clear bush fallow around fields
biological: Metarhizium acridum fungal biopesticide (Green Muscle)
Conserve birds and other predators
chemical: Spot-treat nymph bands with registered products instead of whole fields

edibility.reason: Grasshoppers eat leaves; remaining produce is not made harmful.
advice: Wash produce before eating
Discard badly chewed parts

maize_gray_leaf_spot.description: A fungal leaf disease favoured by warm, humid weather and continuous maize. Severe infections kill leaves before the grain fills.
identification: Rectangular grey to tan lesions bounded by leaf veins
Lesions run parallel to the veins
Starts on lower leaves
symptoms: Lesions merge and blight whole leaves
maize_gray_leaf_spot.lifecycle: Survives on maize residue left on the surface; spores spread by wind and rain splash in humid weather.

cultural: Rotate away from maize for a season
Bury or remove maize residue
Plant tolerant varieties
biological: Balanced fertiliser for vigorous plants
chemical: Registered fungicide at early tasselling only for severe risk

edibility.reason: The fungus attacks leaves; the grain is safe to eat.
advice: Check cobs at harvest and discard any mouldy ones
Dry grain well before storage

maize_leaf_blight.description: A fungal leaf disease favoured by cool, humid weather. Large lesions reduce the leaf area that feeds the cob, lowering yield when it strikes before tasselling.
identification: Long cigar-shaped grey-green to tan lesions, 2-15 cm
Lesions start on lower leaves and move upward
Dark grey spore growth on lesions in humid weather
symptoms: Lesions join and kill whole leaves
Early drying of the plant and smaller cobs
maize_leaf_blight.lifecycle: Survives in infected crop residue. Spores are spread by wind and rain splash to new leaves; infection needs 6-18 hours of leaf wetness.

cultural: Plant resistant or tolerant varieties
Rotate maize with legumes
Bury or remove infected residue after harvest
Avoid very dense planting
biological: Keep plants vigorous with balanced fertiliser
chemical: Fungicide only on high-value or seed crops when lesions appear before tasselling, using registered products

edibility.reason: The fungus attacks leaves, not the grain. Yield may drop but grain is safe.
advice: Check cobs at harvest and discard any mouldy ones
Dry grain well before storage

maize_rust.description: A rust fungus that forms powdery reddish-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces. Usually causes limited loss unless infection is heavy early in the season.
identification: Small oval, raised, cinnamon-brown pustules
Pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Rust-coloured powder rubs off on your fingers
symptoms: Leaves dry early in heavy infection
maize_rust.lifecycle: Spores blow in on the wind; new pustules appear about a week after infection in cool, moist conditions.

cultural: Use resistant varieties
Plant early so the crop matures before peak rust
biological: Maintain good crop nutrition
chemical: Rarely needed on grain maize; consider registered fungicide only for severe early infection

edibility.reason: Rust only infects leaves; it does not make the grain harmful.
advice: Grain is safe; dry well before storage

maize_stem_borer.scientific_name: Busseola fusca, Sesamia calamistis, Eldana saccharina
maize_stem_borer.description: Caterpillars that bore into maize stems and cobs, weakening the plant and cutting off the flow of water and nutrients.
identification: Creamy or pinkish larvae found inside tunnels in the stem
Small round holes on the stem with frass pushed out
Rows of 'shot holes' across leaves as they unroll
symptoms: 'Dead heart': the central shoot dries out on young plants
maize_stem_borer.lifecycle: Eggs laid under leaf sheaths → larvae feed in whorl then bore into stem (3-5 weeks) → pupate in stem → adult moth. Larvae can survive the dry season in old stalks.

cultural: Destroy or chop old stalks after harvest
Early and synchronised planting
Intercrop with cowpea or push-pull with Desmodium
Balanced fertiliser for vigorous plants
biological: Conserve parasitic wasps (Cotesia spp.)
Bt biopesticides on young larvae before they enter the stem
chemical: Treat early, before larvae bore into the stem
Use registered granules or sprays in the whorl as per label

maize_stem_borer.taxonomy: Animalia › Arthropoda › Insecta › Lepidoptera › Noctuidae / Pyralidae

edibility.reason: Borer holes in cobs let in moulds that can produce toxins.
advice: Remove damaged kernels and any larvae
Throw away cobs with visible mould

maize_streak_virus.description: Africa's most important maize virus, spread by Cicadulina leafhoppers. Early infection stunts plants and can cause total loss.
identification: Narrow broken yellow streaks running along the leaf veins
Streaks appear on new leaves after infection
Tiny leafhoppers on plants
symptoms: Small or no cobs when infected young
maize_streak_virus.lifecycle: Leafhoppers pick up the virus from grasses or infected maize and carry it to new plants. There is no cure once a plant is infected.

cultural: Plant MSV-resistant varieties
Avoid late planting next to older maize
Remove grass weeds around fields
Pull out infected young plants
biological: Conserve natural enemies of leafhoppers
chemical: Treated seed or early leafhopper control in high-risk areas, using registered products

edibility.reason: Plant viruses do not infect people. Cobs may be small but are safe.
advice: Grain from infected plants is safe to eat

red_spider_mite.description: Tiny mites that feed on leaf cells and spin fine webs. They build up very fast in hot, dry and dusty conditions.
identification: Red, orange or greenish mites under 0.5 mm
Fine silk webbing on the underside of leaves and between leaves
Best seen with a hand lens
symptoms: Fine yellow or white speckling (stippling) on leaves
Bronzed, dry leaves that fall off
Webbing covering shoot tips in heavy attacks
red_spider_mite.lifecycle: Egg → larva → two nymph stages → adult in 7-12 days in hot weather; each female lays around 100 eggs.

cultural: Keep plants well watered and reduce dust
Remove heavily infested leaves
Avoid pyrethroid sprays, which often cause mite outbreaks
biological: Predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis)
Neem oil or soap sprays on the underside of leaves
chemical: Use a registered acaricide (not a general insecticide) and rotate products

red_spider_mite.taxonomy: Animalia › Arthropoda › Arachnida › Acari › Trombidiformes › Tetranychidae

edibility.reason: Mites weaken the plant but do not make the produce harmful.
advice: Wash produce to remove mites and webbing

thrips.scientific_name: Thrips tabaci, Frankliniella spp., Megalurothrips sjostedti
thrips.description: Very slender, tiny insects that scrape plant surfaces and suck the contents. On cowpea, flower thrips cause flowers to drop.
identification: Slender insects 1-2 mm long, yellow to dark brown
Fringed wings seen with a hand lens
Hide in flowers, leaf sheaths and onion necks
symptoms: Silvery or bronze streaks on leaves
thrips.lifecycle: Egg inside plant tissue → two larval stages → pupa in soil → adult. About 2-3 weeks in warm weather.

cultural: Overhead irrigation or rain reduces numbers
Remove weeds and crop residues
Avoid planting next to infested onion fields
biological: Blue sticky traps for monitoring
Neem-based sprays
Conserve predatory bugs (Orius) and mites
chemical: Spray at flower bud stage for cowpea flower thrips using registered products

edibility.reason: Thrips damage is mostly cosmetic scarring.
advice: Wash well; scarred skin is safe to eat
Discard fruit that is split or rotting

tomato_bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease favoured by warm rain. It spots leaves and fruit and is spread by seed, transplants and splashing water.
identification: Small dark, water-soaked leaf spots, often with yellow halos
Raised, scabby brown spots on green fruit
tomato_bacterial_spot.lifecycle: Carried on seed and plant debris; spreads by rain splash, handling of wet plants and tools.

cultural: Use certified disease-free seed and healthy transplants
Avoid working in wet plants
Rotate crops and remove debris
biological: Resistant varieties where available
chemical: Copper-based registered products can slow spread; follow label

edibility.reason: Spots are on the skin; the bacterium is a plant pathogen, not a human one.
advice: Wash well and cut away spotted skin
Discard fruit that is soft or rotting

tomato_early_blight.description: A common fungal disease that starts on older lower leaves and can reach the fruit, causing dark sunken spots near the stem end.
identification: Brown spots with concentric 'target' rings
Yellow halo around spots
Starts on the oldest leaves
symptoms: Yellowing and leaf drop from the bottom up
Dark leathery sunken spots on fruit near the stem
tomato_early_blight.lifecycle: Survives in soil and plant debris; spores spread by wind and water splash in warm, humid weather.

cultural: Rotate away from tomato-family crops for 2-3 years
Mulch and stake plants to keep leaves off soil
Remove infected lower leaves
Water at the base, not over the leaves
biological: Bacillus subtilis-based biofungicides where available
chemical: Registered protectant fungicides at first symptoms, following the label

edibility.reason: Fruit spots can let in rot organisms.
advice: Cut away small spots generously or discard spotted fruit
Eat only firm, clean fruit

tomato_late_blight.description: A fast-spreading water mould that can destroy a field within days in cool, wet weather. Infected fruit rots.
identification: Large, irregular, greasy grey-green to brown leaf patches
White downy growth under leaves in humid mornings
Firm brown greasy blotches on fruit
symptoms: Rapid browning and collapse of leaves and stems
tomato_late_blight.lifecycle: Spores spread by wind and rain; new infections appear within 3-5 days in cool, moist weather.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately; do not compost
Space and stake plants for air flow
Avoid overhead watering
Do not plant next to potatoes
biological: Use tolerant varieties where available
chemical: Protectant fungicides before and during wet spells, using registered products

edibility.reason: Infected fruit rots quickly and invites other microbes.
advice: Do not eat fruit with brown, greasy blotches — discard it
Unaffected, firm fruit from the same plant can be eaten after washing

tomato_leaf_mold.description: A fungal disease of tomato leaves that thrives in humid, poorly ventilated conditions such as greenhouses and dense plantings.
identification: Pale green to yellow patches on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to brown velvety mould on the underside of the same patches
tomato_leaf_mold.lifecycle: Survives on plant debris and seed; spores spread by air, water and handling when humidity is above about 85%.

cultural: Improve air flow: stake, prune lower leaves, wider spacing
Avoid wetting leaves; water at the base
Remove and destroy infected leaves and crop debris
biological: Grow resistant varieties where available
chemical: Registered protectant fungicides if disease spreads, following the label

edibility.reason: The mould attacks leaves; the fruit is normally not infected and is safe to eat.
advice: Wash fruit before eating
Discard any fruit that is soft or mouldy

tomato_leafminer.description: An invasive moth whose larvae mine inside tomato leaves, stems and fruits. Uncontrolled, it can destroy entire tomato fields.
identification: Small greyish-brown moth about 7 mm long
Pale green to pinkish larvae inside leaf mines
Pin-sized holes in fruit
symptoms: Irregular translucent blotch mines in leaves
Holes and galleries in fruit, often near the calyx
Dried, burnt-looking leaves in heavy attack
tomato_leafminer.lifecycle: Egg → four larval instars inside leaf or fruit → pupa in soil or leaf → adult. Complete cycle in about 3-4 weeks; many generations per year.

cultural: Use clean seedlings from protected nurseries
Remove and destroy infested leaves and fruit
Crop rotation away from tomato family
Destroy crop residues after harvest
biological: Pheromone traps for monitoring and mass trapping
Bt biopesticides and neem-based products
Conserve predatory bugs such as Nesidiocoris
chemical: Use registered products and rotate modes of action; resistance develops quickly

edibility.reason: Larvae tunnel inside the fruit, which then rots easily.
advice: Cut away or discard fruit with holes or tunnels
Eat only firm, undamaged fruit

tomato_mosaic_virus.organism_type: Virus (spread by touch, tools and seed)
tomato_mosaic_virus.description: A very stable virus spread by hands, tools and infected seed. It mottles leaves and can reduce yield and fruit quality.
identification: Light and dark green mosaic mottling on leaves
Leaves may be fern-like, curled or distorted
Uneven ripening or brown streaks in fruit
tomato_mosaic_virus.lifecycle: Survives for long periods in debris and on tools and hands; enters plants through small wounds during handling. No insect is needed.

cultural: Use certified virus-free seed
Remove infected plants
Wash hands and disinfect tools between plants
Do not smoke or handle tobacco while working with plants
biological: Plant resistant varieties
chemical: No chemical cure for the virus

edibility.reason: Plant viruses do not infect people. Blotchy fruit is safe to eat.
advice: Wash fruit before eating

tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.description: A very common fungal leaf spot that starts on lower leaves and can strip plants of foliage, exposing fruit to sunscald.
identification: Many small round spots (2-5 mm) with grey centres and dark borders
Tiny black dots (fruiting bodies) in the spot centres
symptoms: Numerous small leaf spots on lower leaves first
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.lifecycle: Survives on debris and weeds of the tomato family; spores are splashed by rain and irrigation in warm, wet weather.

cultural: Remove infected lower leaves
Mulch to stop soil splash
Rotate crops and destroy debris
Control nightshade weeds
biological: Keep plants well spaced and vigorous
chemical: Registered protectant fungicides at first spots

edibility.reason: Septoria infects leaves, not fruit. Fruit is safe to eat.
advice: Wash fruit before eating
Discard fruit with sunscald that has gone soft

tomato_target_spot.description: A fungal disease of warm, humid regions that causes target-like spots on leaves, stems and fruit.
identification: Brown leaf spots with light-brown concentric rings
Spots often have a yellow halo
Small sunken spots on fruit
tomato_target_spot.lifecycle: Survives on crop debris and many host plants; spores spread by wind and water in warm, wet weather.

cultural: Prune for air flow
Remove infected leaves and debris
Avoid overhead watering
Rotate crops
biological: Keep plants vigorous with balanced nutrition
chemical: Registered fungicides when spots appear, rotating products

edibility.reason: Fruit spots can crack and let rot organisms in.
advice: Cut away spotted areas or discard spotted fruit
Eat only firm, clean fruit

tomato_yellow_leaf_curl.description: A whitefly-transmitted virus that stunts tomato plants and stops them setting fruit when infection is early.
identification: Young leaves small, curled upward and yellow at the edges
Stunted, bushy plants
Whiteflies under leaves
symptoms: Upward leaf curling and yellow margins
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl.lifecycle: Whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) pick up the virus from infected plants and spread it; infected plants cannot be cured.

cultural: Raise seedlings under insect-proof net
Remove infected plants early
Plant tolerant varieties
Avoid planting near old infected crops
biological: Manage whitefly with yellow sticky traps and neem
chemical: Control whitefly early with registered products; the virus itself has no cure

edibility.reason: Plant viruses do not infect people. Any fruit produced is safe.
advice: Wash fruit before eating

whitefly.description: Tiny white flying insects that feed on the underside of leaves. Their biggest damage comes from spreading viruses such as cassava mosaic disease and tomato yellow leaf curl.
identification: White, moth-like insects about 1 mm long
Fly up in a cloud when the plant is shaken
Flat, oval, scale-like nymphs under the leaf
symptoms: Leaf curl, mosaic patterns and stunting from transmitted viruses
whitefly.lifecycle: Egg → four nymph stages → adult in about 3-4 weeks. Adults live for several weeks and lay eggs on young leaves.

cultural: Use virus-free planting material and tolerant varieties
Remove and destroy virus-infected plants early
Avoid planting new crops next to old infested ones
Use insect-proof netting for nurseries
biological: Yellow sticky traps
Neem oil sprays on the underside of leaves
Conserve parasitoid wasps such as Encarsia and Eretmocerus
chemical: Whitefly resists many insecticides quickly; rotate modes of action
Use only registered products and follow extension advice

edibility.reason: Whiteflies feed on leaves; the produce itself is not made harmful.
advice: Wash produce before eating
Fruits from virus-affected plants may be small but are safe

healthy.description: No pest or pest damage was recognised in this image. Keep scouting regularly, because early detection is the cheapest form of control.
identification: Uniform leaf colour
No holes, mines, webbing or insects visible

cultural: Scout your field at least once a week
Keep the field weed-free and remove crop residues
Rotate crops between seasons
biological: Protect natural enemies by avoiding unnecessary sprays
Use sticky or pheromone traps for early warning
chemical: No treatment needed

edibility.reason: No pest, disease or rot was recognised in the photo.
advice: Wash produce before eating as usual
